name: Catching the Machine's Mistakes
title: Catching the Machine's Mistakes
answer: Catching the machine's mistakes is a math activity where students review AI solutions to problems they have already learned, some correct and some wrong, and explain the errors. It matters because students learn that a confident answer is not always a correct one and build the habit of checking answers from any source. The lesson also strengthens their math and their reasoning as they verify each solution.

sections.body: This idea flips the usual use of an AI tool in math class. Rather than asking the tool for help, students act as reviewers of its work. The teacher presents a set of AI solutions to problems the class has already covered, mixing correct answers with errors. Students must find the mistakes and explain exactly where the reasoning went wrong. The problem it solves is the tendency to trust a fluent or confident response without verifying it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a math classroom, the teacher can show the class a set of AI solutions and ask students to check each one. Students solve the problems themselves to see whether the AI answer holds up, then describe the error when it does not. The teacher should know the correct answers before class and can deliberately plant a few errors so the set includes the mistakes students most need to recognize. Older students can also try to make the tool fail and then write up what they found. The activity works across the chapter's kindergarten through twelfth grade span, with older students taking on the additional challenge of probing the tool's limits.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for this idea. It describes a classroom practice and the skills it builds, not a research trial. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. A confident AI answer is not always correct, so students should check any answer, whether it comes from a machine, a website, or a classmate. The teacher keeps the decisions: preparing the sets, knowing the right answers before class, and choosing which errors to plant. Older students may try to make the tool fail, but the written report is their own work and the teacher remains responsible for the lesson. The activity does not remove the need for a person to judge the mathematics and guide the discussion.
